context: Marie Tharp arrived at Columbia University in 1948 «with two master’s degrees, and almost no prospect» of going to sea.

choices.text: with two master’s degrees and almost no prospect
with two master’s degrees; and almost no prospect
with two master’s degrees and, almost no prospect

why.A: "almost no prospect of going to sea" is not an independent clause, so comma + FANBOYS is illegal here.
why.B: Correct — two compound objects of the same preposition need no comma.
why.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence on both sides.
why.D: A comma cannot separate a conjunction from what follows it.

context: Research vessels of the era «do not accept» women aboard, so Tharp worked from a drafting table.

why.A: Present tense clashes with the past-tense "worked" later in the same sentence.
why.B: Future tense is impossible for a historical fact.
why.C: Correct — matches the established past tense of the surrounding narrative.
why.D: Present progressive contradicts the historical setting.

context: For four years she plotted depth readings, «one single line at a time, one after another.»

choices.text: one single line at a time.
OMIT the underlined portion, ending the sentence after "readings."

why.A: "one single" is redundant and "one after another" repeats "at a time."
why.B: "one single" still says the same thing twice.
why.C: Correct — the shortest phrasing that keeps the full meaning.
why.D: This removes the redundancy by removing the information. The sentence exists to say how slowly the plotting went, and "one line at a time" is the only place it says it.

context: «Plotting depth readings for four years, the drafting paper revealed» a mountain range running down the center of the Atlantic.

choices.text: Plotting depth readings for four years, Tharp saw emerge on her drafting paper
Plotted for four years, the depth readings on drafting paper revealed
After four years of plotting depth readings, the paper showed

why.A: Dangling modifier — drafting paper cannot plot readings.
why.B: Correct — places Tharp, the actual plotter, immediately after the modifier.
why.C: Readings do not plot themselves either; the actor is still missing.
why.D: "the paper" still did not do the four years of plotting.

context: Splitting that range lengthwise was a deep V-shaped notch «— a rift valley.»

why.A: Correct — a single dash after a complete clause may introduce an appositive for emphasis.
why.B: Also defensible in isolation, but ACT will not offer two fully correct choices; the dash is what the sentence’s emphatic reveal calls for.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it.
why.D: A closing dash at the end of a sentence is not a real construction.

context: Tharp recognized what the valley implied. If the seafloor was pulling apart along that seam, then continents were moving, «a idea» then associated with Alfred Wegener.

why.A: "a" cannot precede a vowel sound.
why.B: Correct — "an" before the vowel sound in "idea."
why.C: "and" creates a nonsensical list.
why.D: "ideal" changes the meaning entirely.

context: Heezen dismissed her interpretation as "girl talk" and asked her to redraw the maps. «Therefore,» she redrew them. The rift valley appeared again.

why.A: "Therefore" implies the redrawing follows logically as a conclusion, which flattens the passage’s point.
why.B: "Nevertheless" wrongly signals that she redrew them despite being asked to.
why.C: The redrawing is not an example of anything.
why.D: Correct — the two-word sentence lands hardest with no connector, and the sequence is already clear.

context: It appeared in the North Atlantic, «in profiles from the Indian Ocean, and the Pacific was another place it appeared.»

choices.text: in profiles from the Indian Ocean, and in the Pacific.
the Indian Ocean profiles, and appearing in the Pacific.
in the Indian Ocean, also the Pacific.

why.A: The third item switches to a full clause, breaking parallel structure.
why.B: Correct — three parallel prepositional phrases beginning with "in."
why.C: Mixes a noun phrase with a participial phrase.
why.D: "also the Pacific" is not parallel and creates a comma splice feel.

context: When Heezen overlaid the locations of recorded undersea earthquakes onto Tharp’s maps, the pattern of epicenters «trace» the rift valley almost exactly.

why.A: The subject is "pattern," singular, and the passage is in past tense.
why.B: Still plural, and the added pronoun is redundant.
why.C: Correct — singular subject "pattern" plus past tense to match the narrative.
why.D: Present perfect breaks the established past-tense sequence.

stem: The writer is considering deleting the sentence "Heezen dismissed her interpretation as ‘girl talk.’" If deleted, the paragraph would primarily lose:

choices.text: a specific detail that conveys the professional resistance Tharp’s discovery met.
evidence that Heezen was not a competent scientist.
a transition to the paragraph about plate tectonics.
nothing of significance, since the resistance is stated elsewhere.

why.B: The passage never evaluates Heezen’s competence; it later credits his earthquake overlay.
why.C: The sentence does not function as a transition.
why.D: No other sentence states the resistance in specific terms.

context: The maps «Tharp’s and Heezen’s» published in 1957 changed how the public pictured the planet.

why.A: Nothing is possessed here — they are the subject of "published."
why.B: Correct — a compound subject with no possession requires no apostrophe.
why.C: Adds incorrect plurals to proper names.
why.D: Introduces a possessive where none belongs.

context: Plate tectonics, the framework that now organizes all of geology, «rests substantially on» the seafloor she drew.

why.A: Correct — matches the passage’s measured, formal register.
why.B: "totally built off of" is colloquial and overstated.
why.C: "kind of" is vague and informal.
why.D: "a whole lot" clashes with the surrounding academic prose.

No, because it does not explain the mechanism of plate tectonics in detail.

why.B: Only one woman is discussed.
why.C: The obstacles are secondary; the contribution is the spine of the essay.
why.D: A detailed mechanism was never part of the stated goal.

context: They are met by a dozen volunteers with soldering irons, sewing machines, and «a rule; nobody repairs anything for you.»

a rule, nobody repairs anything for you.
a rule nobody repairs anything for you.

why.B: Correct — a colon announces the rule that follows, and the clause before it is complete.
why.C: Creates a comma splice.
why.D: Runs two statements together with no punctuation.

context: «I starting coming two years ago» with a toaster that had stopped toasting.

choices.text: I started coming two years ago
Starting to come two years ago
Having started coming two years ago

why.B: Correct — supplies a real past-tense main verb.
why.C: Leaves the sentence with no main verb at all.

context: Ellis, «a retired elevator mechanic handed» me a screwdriver and waited.

why.A: The nonessential appositive opens with a comma but never closes.
why.B: Correct — matched pair of commas around the appositive.
why.C: A semicolon cannot close an appositive.
why.D: A dash cannot close what a comma opened.

context: Inside was not the mysterious machinery I expected, «it was a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.»

a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal it was.
it being a spring, a lever, and a corroded strip of metal.

why.A: Comma splice — two independent clauses joined by only a comma.

why.C: Awkward inversion that still leaves a splice.
why.D: A participial phrase that garbles the sentence.

context: We cleaned the contact. The toaster «has worked» for another three years.

why.A: Present perfect implies the toaster is still working, but "another three years" is a closed period.
why.B: Present tense contradicts the completed span.
why.C: Correct — simple past for a finished duration.
why.D: Future tense is impossible for an event already described.

context: A toaster costs sixteen dollars, and I «had been prepared and ready to throw one away in the garbage» rather than spend twenty minutes with a screwdriver.

choices.text: had been prepared to throw one away
was prepared and ready to discard one
had been ready to throw one away in the trash

why.A: "prepared and ready" is redundant, as is "away in the garbage."
why.B: Correct — removes both redundancies without losing meaning.
why.C: Still doubles "prepared and ready."
why.D: "throw away in the trash" repeats itself.

context: The economics were not the point; the habit was. «In addition,» the Repair Café movement began in Amsterdam in 2009 and has since spread to more than two thousand locations.

why.A: "In addition" implies the new paragraph adds to the previous point, but it shifts to background information.
why.B: The movement’s founding is not a consequence of the writer’s realization.
why.C: Correct — the paragraph turns to context and needs no connector.

context: Its organizers keep careful records: what came in, what was fixed, what could not be. «Roughly two-thirds of items leaves» working.

choices.text: Roughly two-thirds of items is leaving
Roughly two-thirds of items has left

why.A: With fractions, the verb agrees with the object of "of" — "items" is plural.
why.B: Correct — plural verb for a plural object.
why.C: Singular and needlessly progressive.
why.D: Singular and shifts tense.

context: The remaining third leave with an explanation, «which the volunteers insist it is also a kind of success.»

choices.text: which the volunteers insist is also a kind of success.
that the volunteers insist it is also a kind of success.
and the volunteers insist is also a kind of success.

why.A: "which" already serves as the clause’s subject, so "it" is a redundant second subject.
why.B: Correct — removes the doubled subject.
why.C: Same doubled-subject error, and "that" would require no comma.
why.D: Leaves the clause without a clear subject.

stem: The writer wants to add the sentence "He never once took the screwdriver out of my hand." Where would it most logically be placed?

In paragraph 2, after "Ellis... handed me a screwdriver and waited."

context: The café now runs a small-appliance table «in his name, staffed from three people» he taught.

choices.text: in his name, staffed by three people
on his name, staffed by three people
in his name, staffed with three people

why.C: "on his name" is not idiomatic.

stem: Which choice best concludes the essay by tying back to its opening image of broken things?
context: Final sentence options:

choices.text: I am not a good repairer. I am a patient one, which he told me is most of the job.
Repair Cafés can be found in over two thousand locations worldwide.
Ellis was seventy-eight when he died, and he had worked on elevators for forty years.

why.A: Correct — returns to the essay’s personal thread and to Ellis’s lesson about the nature of repair.
why.B: A statistic already given, with no connection to the closing image.
why.C: Biographical detail that does not resolve the essay’s idea.
why.D: A generic moral that abandons the specific voice of the piece.

context: The trees grew a hundred feet tall «and eight feet across, produced reliable annual nut crops, and yielded» straight, rot-resistant timber.

and eight feet across; produced reliable annual nut crops; and yielded
and eight feet across, produced reliable annual nut crops and, yielded

why.A: Correct — three parallel verbs in a series, properly separated by commas.
why.B: Removing the commas fuses the list into unreadable prose.
why.C: Semicolons are only for list items that themselves contain commas.
why.D: Places a comma between the conjunction and its verb.

context: «Cryphonectria parasitica, a fungus that had arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.» Asian chestnuts had coevolved with it and tolerated it.

Cryphonectria parasitica being a fungus that had arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.
Cryphonectria parasitica, a fungus, having arrived on imported Japanese chestnut stock.

why.A: A noun followed by an appositive with no main verb is a fragment.
why.B: Correct — supplies subject and verb ("The cause was").
why.C: "being" is not a conjugated main verb.
why.D: Still a fragment, now with an extra dangling appositive.

context: Asian chestnuts had coevolved with the fungus and tolerated it. American chestnuts had not. «This» moved outward at roughly twenty-four miles a year.

why.A: "This" has no clear antecedent — it could point to the fungus, the tolerance, or the whole situation.
why.B: Plural and equally vague.
why.C: Correct — naming the noun removes the ambiguity.
why.D: "It" could refer to the fungus or to either chestnut species.

context: Within forty years an estimated four billion trees «are» dead.

why.A: Present tense clashes with the completed historical span.
why.B: Correct — simple past matches the narrative of the blight’s spread.
why.C: Present perfect suggests the dying continues into the present.
why.D: Future tense is impossible for a completed event.

context: Most Americans alive today have never seen a mature chestnut. The species, «therefore,» is not extinct.

why.A: Extinction does not follow from people not having seen the tree.
why.B: Correct — signals the contrast between apparent total loss and continued survival.
why.C: Survival is not an addition to the loss; it opposes it.
why.D: The survival is not an example of the loss.

context: Millions of these stump sprouts «persists» across the Appalachians.

why.A: "Millions" is plural, so the singular verb is wrong.
why.B: Correct — plural subject takes a plural verb.
why.C: Singular and shifts the tense unnecessarily.
why.D: Singular and needlessly progressive.

context: «Girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, an estimated four billion trees were killed by the blight.»

choices.text: Girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, the blight killed an estimated four billion trees.
Girdled trunks and cut nutrient flow killed an estimated four billion trees.
An estimated four billion trees, girdling trunks and cutting off nutrient flow, died.

why.B: Correct — places "the blight," which does the girdling, right after the modifier.
why.C: Changes the meaning and drops the blight as the agent.
why.D: Attaches the modifier to the trees, repeating the original error.

context: Breeders cross American chestnuts with Chinese varieties and then «backcrossing the hybrids» repeatedly toward American characteristics.

why.A: "cross... and backcrossing" mixes a conjugated verb with a participle.
why.B: Correct — both verbs share the subject "Breeders" in the same form.
why.C: An infinitive does not parallel "cross."

stem: The writer is considering adding: "Chestnut wood was also prized by furniture makers in the nineteenth century." Should the sentence be added to the final paragraph?

Yes, because it provides a transition to the restoration efforts.

why.B: Correct — the concise standard form.

context: A member can «borrow a tile saw for a weekend, return it on Monday, and pay nothing» beyond the annual fee.

borrow a tile saw for a weekend, return it on Monday, and paying nothing
borrowing a tile saw for a weekend, return it on Monday, and pay nothing

the shelves, crowded from floor to ceiling, holds now

context: … a sewing machine that three separate members «learned» to use last spring.

why.A: "Last spring" places the action in a finished period, and the simple past is the tense for a finished period.
why.B: The present perfect resists a specific finished time. "Have learned last spring" is not idiomatic English.
why.C: The future perfect places the action ahead of a future moment, which contradicts "last spring" outright.
why.D: The simple present would describe a habit or a general truth, not something that happened in one named season.

context: The collection began with a single donated item«:» a wheelbarrow with a cracked handle.

why.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses. "A wheelbarrow with a cracked handle" has no verb, so nothing can stand on the right of one.

context: A homeowner who buys a pressure washer uses it perhaps twice a «year, the» same machine, shared, runs most weekends from April to October.

why.A: Both halves are complete sentences. A semicolon is the mark that joins two of those while keeping the contrast tight.
why.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice — the most tested error on the section.
why.C: Removing the punctuation turns the splice into a fused sentence, which is worse rather than better.
why.D: "Therefore" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join two clauses. The comma splice survives underneath it.

context: Donations arrive faster than the volunteers can catalog «them. Which is why» a backlog now fills the hallway.

context: The writer wants to add the sentence "They had expected the saw and the ladder to move; they had not expected the conversations." Where should it go?

context: Every morning at low tide I walked the same hundred metres of shelf «with a laminated card, and counted» what was in the pools.

why.C: Adds a second comma that encloses "and", which is not an interruption.
why.D: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side, and "counted what was in the pools" has no subject of its own.

context: The columns of figures in the nineteen binders «tells» a story no single morning could.

why.A: "To" takes an object, so the pronoun is "me". Drop the other person and the ear settles it: she showed the binders to me.
why.B: "I" is the subject form, and nothing here needs a second subject.
why.C: A reflexive needs a matching subject in the same clause. The subject is "she", so "myself" has nothing to reflect.

context: Every morning I counted the pools, and every afternoon I «was taking school groups» over the same ground.

why.C: A comma here reads as though a list is starting, and then only one item arrives.

, eleven one morning, twelve the next —
— eleven one morning, twelve the next

context: Twelve stars one morning, eleven the next, thirteen the morning after that. «A column of figures that looked like a very slow way of proving nothing.»

why.C: A comma between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
why.D: "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so the splice survives underneath it.

why.B: Five words for a single causal connective.
why.C: The same padding with a different opening word.
why.D: Longer still, and "in light of" suggests weighing evidence rather than stating a cause.

context: Marisol «was super chill about» letting me think this for three weeks.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to explain why long-running measurement programs are worth continuing. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows a nineteen-year record revealing changes no single season could have shown.

context: «Dolores Nakata, who has painted signs by hand for fifty-one years,» is the only person on Ellis Street who still does.

Dolores Nakata who has painted signs by hand for fifty-one years,
Dolores Nakata who has painted signs by hand for fifty-one years

why.B: Opens the interruption and never closes it, so "is the only person" is left stranded inside the clause.
why.C: Closes an interruption that was never opened.
why.D: Without commas the clause reads as restrictive, implying there is another Dolores Nakata who has not painted signs for fifty-one years.

context: She is not sentimental «about» this, which surprises people who come to interview her.

why.A: "Sentimental about" is the fixed pairing in English. Idiom questions have no rule behind them beyond what the language settled on.
why.B: "Sentimental on" is not an English collocation.
why.C: "Sentimental for" reverses the sense toward longing for something rather than having feelings about it.
why.D: "Sentimental with" would describe how she treats a person, not what she feels about a situation.

context: For the last nine years she «is» the only person on Ellis Street who still letters by hand.

why.A: "For the last nine years" runs from the past into the present, and the present perfect is the tense built for that span.
why.B: The simple present describes now only, and cannot carry a nine-year stretch.
why.C: The simple past would place the whole span in a finished period and imply she no longer is.
why.D: The future contradicts a period that has already elapsed.

context: The vocabulary of the trade, along with the tools it names, «have» mostly gone out of the language.

why.A: "Along with" does not create a compound subject. The subject is still the singular "vocabulary".
why.B: The plural verb is agreeing with "tools", which sits inside a parenthetical phrase rather than in the subject.
why.C: "Were" is plural and also shifts the sentence out of the perfect that "gone" requires.
why.D: "Are" is plural, and "are gone out" is not an English construction.

context: She spends her weekdays «setting type on a screen and her Saturdays to work in the shop».

choices.text: setting type on a screen and her Saturdays working in the shop
to set type on a screen and her Saturdays working in the shop
setting type on a screen and her Saturdays she works in the shop

why.A: "Spends X doing, and Y doing" — both halves need the same gerund form for the shared verb to reach them.
why.B: "To work" is an infinitive where the first half used a gerund, so the two halves no longer match.
why.C: Fixes the second half and breaks the first, which leaves the sentence exactly as unparallel.
why.D: Turns the second half into a clause with its own subject and verb, which "spends" can no longer govern.

context: «Spaced by eye against the actual wall, a printer cannot make these decisions.»

choices.text: Spaced by eye against the actual wall, the letters reflect decisions a printer cannot make.
Spacing by eye against the actual wall, a printer cannot make these decisions.
Spaced by eye against the actual wall, these decisions cannot be made by a printer.

why.A: The letters are what gets spaced by eye, so the letters must follow the opening phrase.
why.B: As written, the printer is the thing spaced by eye against the wall.
why.C: "Spacing" makes the printer the one doing the spacing, which is precisely what the passage denies it can do.
why.D: Now the decisions are what was spaced by eye, which is no closer to the meaning.

context: «The reason that she charges more is because» the work takes longer and no one else can do it.

choices.text: The reason for her charging more is on account of
The reason why she charges more is due to the fact that

why.A: Four words instead of seven, and the cause is stated once rather than twice.
why.B: "The reason … is because" says the causal relationship twice over, once in "reason" and again in "because".
why.C: Swaps "because" for "on account of" and keeps the doubled cause, while adding a nominalization.
why.D: Longer than the original and still doubles the cause, now with "why" and "due to the fact that".

context: The trade has a vocabulary of its own«:» the layout, the pounce pattern, the fitch and the quill.

why.A: A complete sentence on the left, a list on the right — which is the standard job of a colon.
why.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on the right, and a list of nouns is not one.
why.C: A comma makes "the layout" look like the first of several things the trade has, rather than the first item of the vocabulary.
why.D: "Namely" does not change what a semicolon needs on its right.

context: She has taught the words to four apprentices «— three of whom now work in other trades».

choices.text: — three of whom now work in other trades —
, three of who now work in other trades
; three of whom now work in other trades

why.A: A single dash can introduce a trailing addition at the end of a sentence. Nothing follows it, so nothing needs closing.
why.B: A closing dash promises the sentence continues, and it does not.
why.C: "Who" is the subject form; here the pronoun is the object of "of", so it has to be "whom".
why.D: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on its right, and this is a relative clause.

context: Nakata learned the words from a man «who» had learned them in the 1930s.

why.A: The pronoun is the subject of "had learned", and the subject form is "who".
why.B: "Whom" is the object form. Test it by substituting he/him: *he* had learned them, so "who".
why.C: "Which" refers to things, and the antecedent here is a man.
why.D: "Whose" is possessive and would need a noun after it.

context: Three of the four apprentices now work in other trades. «Similarly,» the fourth has stayed.

why.A: Three left and one stayed. The second sentence exists to mark the exception, and "by contrast" is the signal for an exception.
why.B: "Similarly" claims the fourth did what the other three did, which is the reverse of the fact.
why.C: "As a result" claims the fourth stayed because the others left, a causal link the passage never draws.
why.D: Three left and one stayed is a contrast, and deleting the transition asks the reader to supply it. The sentence reads as a fourth item in a list instead of an exception to one.

context: Nakata «doesn’t get all misty about» the decline of her trade.

why.A: The article’s register is measured throughout, and "not sentimental" states the point plainly.
why.B: "Gets all misty" is colloquial in a way nothing else in the piece is.
why.C: Casual in the same way, and it also softens the claim from "unsentimental" to "not very troubled".
why.D: Refusing to acknowledge a decline is a different claim — and a false one, since she describes vinyl’s advantages herself.

context: The writer wants to place the sentence "A notice about parking does not need to be beautiful." Where does it best belong?

choices.text: Immediately after "cheaper and faster is the correct answer."
As the opening sentence of the passage.
In the paragraph describing the trade’s vocabulary.
As the last sentence of the passage.

why.A: It is the concrete case for the concession just made. Placed there, it shows what "most of what a sign has to do" covers.
why.B: Opening on parking notices would put a supporting example before anything it supports.
why.C: That paragraph is about the layout, the pounce pattern and the quill, and a parking notice has nothing to do with them.
why.D: The passage ends on the trade’s survival. A concession about parking notices would undercut the close for no reason.

context: The writer is considering deleting the sentence "Vinyl is cheaper and faster, she says, and for most of what a sign has to do, cheaper and faster is the correct answer." Should it be deleted?

choices.text: No, because it establishes that her argument is a narrow one rather than a defence of hand-lettering in general.
No, because it gives the price difference between vinyl and painted work.
Yes, because it contradicts her decision to go on painting.
Yes, because the comparison with vinyl has already been made in the previous paragraph.

why.A: Everything after it depends on the concession. Without it the paragraph that begins "What she argues for is narrower" has nothing to be narrower than.
why.B: The price comparison is in the first paragraph. This sentence gives no figures.
why.C: It does not contradict her; it is what makes her position defensible rather than nostalgic.
why.D: The previous paragraph compares cost and speed. This sentence concedes the point, which is different work.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to show that a craft can survive by doing what its replacement cannot. Would this passage accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it hands the ordinary work to vinyl and locates the craft’s value on site.
Yes, because it reports how many years Nakata has worked.
No, because it concedes that vinyl is cheaper and faster than anything cut by hand in the shop.
No, because three of her four apprentices left the trade for steadier work.

why.A: The third paragraph names what a printer cannot do — space letters by eye, in the real light, at the real reading distance — and the fourth apprentice’s testimony confirms the skill transfers rather than expires.
why.B: Fifty-one years measures her career, not what the craft can do that vinyl cannot.
why.C: The concession is what makes the argument work. A claim that survives an honest concession is stronger, not weaker.
why.D: The fourth stayed, and the closing paragraph treats the trade as having outlasted several announcements of its death.

context: Ellery «disagreed to the assumption» that traffic would keep growing at four percent a year forever.

why.A: "Disagree to" is not an English construction. You agree to a proposal, but you disagree with a claim or a person.
why.B: "Disagree with" is the idiom. The preposition is fixed by usage, not by the meaning of the parts.
why.C: "Disagree from" borrows the preposition that belongs to "differ from".
why.D: "Disagree against" doubles the opposition, since disagreement is already an opposing stance.

context: By 1985 the bridge «carries» fewer cars than it had when she started counting.

why.A: The present tense clashes with "By 1985" and with "had when she started", both of which place the sentence in the past.
why.B: The past progressive matches "By 1985" and sits correctly against the past perfect "had" later in the sentence.
why.C: The future tense describes something still to come, but 1985 has already passed in the essay.
why.D: The present perfect connects a past event to now, which contradicts the fixed past date.

context: «Standing at the east abutment with a tally counter in each hand, the totals were recorded» in a hardbound ledger.

choices.text: Standing at the east abutment with a tally counter in each hand, she recorded the totals
The totals, standing at the east abutment with a tally counter in each hand, were recorded
Standing at the east abutment with a tally counter in each hand, the ledger recorded the totals

why.A: The opening phrase describes a person standing, but the subject that follows is "the totals", which cannot stand anywhere.
why.B: The subject right after the phrase is "she", and she is the one standing. The modifier now attaches to what it describes.
why.C: Moving the phrase into the middle does not change what it modifies — it still reaches for "the totals".
why.D: This gives the ledger the tally counters and the standing, which is no better than giving them to the totals.

context: The city engineers and «her» disagreed about how wide the replacement bridge should be.

why.A: "Her" is an object form, and this word is part of the compound subject doing the disagreeing.
why.B: Strip the sentence to one subject and the ear settles it: "she disagreed", not "her disagreed".
why.C: "Hers" is a possessive standing in for a noun, and nothing here is being possessed.
why.D: A reflexive needs an earlier mention of the same person in the sentence to point back to.

context: Ellery counted the cars, recorded the totals, and «was keeping» the ledgers in a consistent hand.

why.A: The first two items are simple past verbs. A past progressive in the third slot breaks the pattern the list has set.
why.B: "Counted, recorded, and kept" — three simple past verbs, all in the same form.
why.C: The past perfect progressive puts the third item further back in time than the other two, which the sentence does not intend.
why.D: "Would keep" shifts into a conditional or habitual mood the other two items are not in.

context: The eleven volumes of pencil in a consistent hand «is» now in the municipal archive.

why.A: The subject is "volumes", which is plural. "Pencil" is inside a prepositional phrase and cannot govern the verb.
why.B: "The eleven volumes ... are" — the verb matches the plural subject across the intervening phrase.
why.C: "Was" is singular as well as past, so it disagrees on both counts with a plural subject and the present-tense "now".
why.D: "Has been" is singular, and it is the nearest noun rather than the subject that makes it sound acceptable.

context: She stood at the east abutment «with a mechanical tally counter, in each hand» and recorded the totals.

choices.text: with a mechanical tally counter in each hand
with a mechanical tally counter in each hand,
with a mechanical, tally counter in each hand

why.A: The comma splits a prepositional phrase from the phrase that completes it, separating "counter" from where the counters were.
why.B: No comma belongs anywhere inside this phrase, and none belongs before "and", which joins two verbs sharing one subject.
why.C: A comma before "and recorded" would announce a second independent clause, but no new subject follows.
why.D: "Mechanical tally counter" is a single stacked description, not two coordinate adjectives, so no comma separates them.

context: The new bridge is six lanes wide, and «it has never at any time in its history carried» six lanes of traffic.

choices.text: it has not ever at any point carried
there has never been a time when it carried

why.A: "Never", "at any time" and "in its history" all say the same thing. Only one of them is doing any work.
why.B: "Has never carried" says everything the long version says, in three words.
why.C: This swaps one redundant phrase for another without removing the redundancy.
why.D: This turns a direct statement into an "there has been" construction, adding words and burying the verb.

context: In 1979 the growth «stopped, in 1981 it reversed».

why.A: Two complete sentences joined by nothing but a comma — the classic comma splice.
why.B: A semicolon is exactly what joins two closely related independent clauses with no conjunction.
why.C: This moves 1981 onto the wrong clause, saying the growth stopped in 1981, and still splices what follows.
why.D: Adding a second comma makes "in 1981" look like an interruption and leaves the two sentences still spliced.

context: For every crossing, the ledger recorded«: the date, the direction, and the count».

choices.text: the date, the direction, and the count
; the date, the direction, and the count
the date: the direction, and the count

why.A: A colon must follow a complete sentence. "The ledger recorded" is not complete — "recorded" is still waiting for its object.
why.B: The list is the direct object of "recorded", so it attaches straight to the verb with no punctuation at all.
why.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and a three-item list is not a sentence.
why.D: This puts a colon in the middle of the list, separating the first item from the other two for no reason.

context: The new bridge «— built to the original specification —» has never carried six lanes of traffic.

why.A: A pair of dashes sets off an interruption, and the pair is matched: a dash opens it and a dash closes it.
why.B: Opening with a dash and closing with a comma mixes the two marks. Whichever is used has to be used at both ends.
why.C: Same mismatch in the other direction — a comma cannot open what a dash closes.
why.D: With no punctuation at all, "The new bridge built to the original specification" reads as one noun phrase and the interruption disappears.

context: The plans were drawn and the money was appropriated. «Therefore,» Ellery drove out before dawn and counted the cars anyway.

why.A: "Therefore" claims the counting followed from the plans being settled, but the settled plans are the reason not to count.
why.B: The word "anyway" at the end of the sentence already signals a contrast, and "Still" is the transition that matches it.
why.C: "Likewise" claims the second sentence is a parallel case, and counting cars is not parallel to appropriating money.
why.D: "In addition" adds an item to a list, but this sentence works against the previous one rather than extending it.

context: Ellery is «careless» about how she tells this story, and she does not claim she was right and the engineers were wrong.

why.A: "Careless" means the opposite of what the rest of the sentence shows: someone declining to overclaim is being precise, not sloppy.
why.B: "Careful" matches the restraint the sentence goes on to describe.
why.C: "Carefree" means untroubled, which says nothing about how precisely she tells it.
why.D: "Caring" describes warmth toward people, not precision about a claim.

context: The writer is considering deleting the clause "and the plans were drawn, and the money was appropriated" from the first paragraph. Should it be kept?

choices.text: Kept, because it establishes that the decision was already settled, which is what makes the counting look pointless at the time.
Kept, because it tells the reader what year the original bridge was built.
Deleted, because the essay is about traffic counts rather than about construction financing.
Deleted, because it repeats information the paragraph has already given.

why.A: The essay turns on the counting having no official purpose. Without the settled plans and the appropriated money, there is nothing for the counting to be pointless against.
why.B: The paragraph gives 1974 as the replacement date, not the construction date, and the deleted clause does not supply either.
why.C: The financing is what shows the decision was closed, so it is doing work for the essay rather than wandering from it.
why.D: Nothing earlier in the paragraph mentions the plans or the money, so the clause is not a repetition.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to show why a forecast has to be checked against what actually happened. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it sets a four-percent growth model against an eleven-year record showing the opposite.
Yes, because it describes the mechanical tally counters that Ellery held in each hand at the roadside.
No, because the essay concerns a single bridge and never once uses the word forecast.
No, because Ellery herself signed the report that recommended the replacement.

why.A: This names the two things the essay puts in opposition — a projection and a record — and the point Ellery draws from the gap between them.
why.B: The counters are a detail of method. They show how she counted, not why checking a projection matters.
why.C: One extended case is a normal way to make a general point, and the essay states the general point outright in its final lines.
why.D: Her agreement with the replacement is what keeps her narrower claim credible; it does not undercut the essay’s purpose.

context: The eleven dishes she cooked for fifty years «was» never written down.

why.A: "Was" is singular, and the subject is "the eleven dishes".
why.B: "The eleven dishes ... were" — a plural subject takes a plural verb, whatever comes between them.
why.C: "Has been" is also singular, and the relative clause between subject and verb does not change what the verb must agree with.
why.D: "Is" is singular and present, so it disagrees in number and clashes with the past-tense "cooked".

context: My grandmother and «me» spent four weekends in her kitchen with a scale and a notebook.

why.A: "Me" is an object form, and this word is half of the compound subject that does the spending.
why.B: Drop the other half and the choice is obvious: "I spent four weekends", not "me spent four weekends".
why.C: "Myself" is reflexive and needs an earlier "I" in the sentence to refer back to.
why.D: "Mine" is possessive and replaces a noun, which is not what this slot needs.

context: By the time I turned twenty-six, she «makes» the same eleven dishes for half a century.

why.A: The present tense cannot describe something that had already run for fifty years before a past moment.
why.B: The past perfect progressive is built for exactly this: an action running up to a point in the past.
why.C: The present progressive places the cooking now, not before the writer turned twenty-six.
why.D: The future perfect looks forward from the present, and "By the time I turned" looks back.

context: «Weighing what she reached for before she put it in the pot, the measurements were astonishingly consistent.»

choices.text: Weighing what she reached for before she put it in the pot, I found the measurements astonishingly consistent.
The measurements, weighing what she reached for before she put it in the pot, were astonishingly consistent.
Weighing what she reached for before she put it in the pot, the consistency was astonishing.

why.A: The opening phrase needs someone doing the weighing, and the subject that arrives is "the measurements", which did no weighing.
why.B: "I" follows the phrase and "I" did the weighing, so the modifier finally has something to attach to.
why.C: Relocating the phrase changes nothing — it still modifies "the measurements".
why.D: This hands the weighing to "the consistency", which is an abstraction and cannot hold a scale.

context: Garlic burns at a lower temperature than onion does, so it is «susceptible of» turning bitter.

why.A: "Susceptible of" survives in legal and technical writing meaning "admits of", but it is not the idiom for being vulnerable to something.
why.B: "Susceptible to" is the standard idiom for being liable to suffer something.
why.C: "Susceptible for" is not an English pairing.
why.D: "Susceptible with" is not an English pairing either.

context: She learned the sequence by standing beside her mother, by watching her hands, and «she repeated it» for six decades.

why.A: The first two items are "by" plus a gerund. A full clause in the third slot leaves the list half-built.
why.B: "By standing, by watching, and by repeating" — all three items now take the same shape.
why.C: Dropping "by" leaves a bare past-tense verb, which does not match two prepositional phrases.
why.D: "Having repeated" is a perfect participle, which marks the repeating as finished before the learning rather than part of it.

context: I have the eleven recipes now, written in «my grandmothers hand» and annotated in mine.

why.A: The hand belongs to the grandmother, and possession needs an apostrophe.
why.B: One grandmother, so the apostrophe goes before the s.
why.C: An apostrophe after the s marks a plural possessive, but the essay describes one grandmother.
why.D: This stacks two apostrophes, which no possessive form in English uses.

context: My grandmother«, who was eighty-three that year» had decided long ago that nothing needed writing down.

why.A: The clause is set off at the front but never closed, so the comma opens an interruption the sentence does not finish.
why.B: A nonessential clause takes a comma at both ends — remove what sits between them and the sentence still stands.
why.C: Closing without opening is the same error in the other direction.
why.D: With no commas the clause reads as essential, implying the writer has other grandmothers and means the eighty-three-year-old one.

context: She was not improvising. «Executing a recipe she had run several thousand times.»

choices.text: She was executing a recipe she had run several thousand times.
Executing a recipe, she had run several thousand times.
A recipe she had run several thousand times, executing it.

why.A: "Executing" is a participle, not a verb with a subject, so this group of words has no main clause.
why.B: Adding the subject and the helping verb turns the participle into a predicate and the fragment into a sentence.
why.C: The comma makes "she had run several thousand times" the main clause and leaves the recipe with no object to attach to.
why.D: This reorders the fragment without ever supplying a subject and a main verb.

context: What she could not do was «to give an explanation of the reason why» the onions went in before the garlic.

choices.text: give an explanation as to the reason
explain the reason as to why

why.A: "Give an explanation of the reason why" takes seven words to say what "explain why" says in two.
why.B: "Explain why" carries the whole meaning, and the verb does the work the noun phrase was doing.
why.C: This trades one padded phrase for another and drops the "why" the sentence still needs.
why.D: "The reason as to why" stacks three ways of saying the same thing.

context: Her cupped hand was more consistent than most people manage with a measuring cup. «For example,» she could not say how much it held.

why.A: Not being able to state the amount is not an example of being consistent; it works against it.
why.B: "Even so" concedes the first sentence and then sets the limitation against it, which is the relation here.
why.C: "Therefore" claims the inability follows from the consistency, and it does not.
why.D: The essay turns on the gap between doing a thing well and being able to say how, so the concession has to be marked. Deleted, the two sentences read as unrelated observations.

context: I am not sure this is an improvement so much as a translation; the notebook has «affected» a change in where the knowledge lives.

why.A: "Affect" as a verb means to influence something that already exists. The sentence needs the sense of bringing the change about.
why.B: "Effect" used as a verb means to bring about, which is exactly what a change requires here.
why.C: The bare form does not fit after "has", which needs a past participle.
why.D: "Effect" as a noun cannot follow "has" in this construction either.

context: The measurements were astonishingly consistent «— ninety-two grams, then ninety, then ninety-four —» which is a tighter tolerance than most cooks manage.

choices.text: — ninety-two grams, then ninety, then ninety-four,
, ninety-two grams, then ninety, then ninety-four —
ninety-two grams, then ninety, then ninety-four

why.A: The readings interrupt the sentence and a matched pair of dashes sets them off — which is also the clearest mark to use when the interruption itself contains commas.
why.B: A dash at one end and a comma at the other leaves the pair unmatched.
why.C: Same mismatch reversed, and a comma cannot open an interruption that already contains commas without confusing the reader.
why.D: With no punctuation the three readings run straight into the sentence and the reader cannot tell where the interruption ends.

context: The writer is considering adding the sentence "Garlic burns at a lower temperature than onion and turns bitter." Should it be added?

choices.text: Yes, because it supplies the reason the writer’s grandmother followed correctly without being able to state it.
Yes, because it explains why the writer decided to buy a kitchen scale.
No, because the essay never otherwise mentions garlic.
No, because it contradicts the claim that the grandmother got the sequence right every time.

why.A: The whole essay turns on a rule that worked without a stated reason. The sentence is that missing reason, and the gap it fills is the essay’s subject.
why.B: The scale was bought to record quantities, and nothing about garlic chemistry bears on that decision.
why.C: The garlic and onion sequence is exactly what the writer asks about and cannot get an answer to.
why.D: It explains why her sequence was right. Supplying the reason for a correct rule does not contradict its correctness.

context: Suppose the writer had intended to examine the difference between knowing how to do something and being able to explain it. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.text: Yes, because it shows a cook running a sequence reliably for sixty years without being able to say why it worked.
Yes, because it lists all eleven of the dishes the grandmother made without ever writing down a recipe for any of them.
No, because the essay is about recipes rather than about knowledge of any kind.
No, because the writer eventually located the reason in a textbook.

why.A: This names both halves of the distinction and the single person who displays the gap between them.
why.B: The essay never lists the dishes, and a list would show what she cooked rather than what she knew.
why.C: The recipes are the occasion. What the essay actually examines is what was and was not transmitted along with them.
why.D: Finding the reason afterward is what makes the gap visible — it shows the rule was right and the explanation was simply missing.

context: A watershed that once released its rainfall over several days now «release» it in a few hours.

why.A: The subject is the singular "a watershed". The relative clause between it and the verb does not change what the verb agrees with.
why.B: "A watershed ... releases" — singular subject, singular verb.
why.C: "Have released" is plural and shifts to the present perfect, neither of which the sentence supports.
why.D: "Are releasing" is plural as well, and the nearest noun, "days", is not the subject.

context: For most of the twentieth century, the guiding principle of urban drainage «is» speed.

why.A: The present tense contradicts "For most of the twentieth century", which closes the period off in the past.
why.B: A completed stretch of past time takes the simple past.
why.C: The present perfect would mean the principle still governs, which is what the rest of the passage argues has changed.
why.D: The future tense places the principle ahead of us rather than behind us.

context: Cities had not eliminated «they’re» flooding; they had exported it downstream.

why.A: "They’re" is a contraction of "they are", which gives "had not eliminated they are flooding".
why.B: "Their" is the possessive form, and the flooding belongs to the cities.
why.C: "There" points at a place and cannot show possession.
why.D: "Theirs" stands alone in place of a noun and cannot sit in front of one.

context: The older designs paved the channel, straightened the creek, and «the water was buried» in a culvert.

why.A: The first two items are active past-tense verbs with the designs as subject. The third switches to a passive clause with a different subject.
why.B: "Paved, straightened, and buried" — three active past-tense verbs sharing one subject.
why.C: A gerund does not match two finite verbs.
why.D: A noun phrase cannot sit in a list whose other members are verbs.

context: «Ignored for three years, a city discovers that a rain garden becomes a weed patch that does not drain.»

choices.text: A rain garden ignored for three years becomes a weed patch that does not drain.
Ignored for three years, the discovery is that a rain garden becomes a weed patch that does not drain.
A city, ignored for three years, discovers that a rain garden becomes a weed patch that does not drain.

why.A: The opening phrase lands on "a city", so the sentence says the city was ignored for three years rather than the garden.
why.B: The phrase now sits directly against "a rain garden", which is the thing actually being ignored.
why.C: This attaches the neglect to "the discovery", which is no more capable of being ignored for three years than the city was.
why.D: Moving the phrase into commas after "a city" states outright what the original merely implied — that the city was ignored.

context: The newer designs are «different than» the older ones in one respect above all.

why.A: "Different than" is common in speech but is not the form tested as standard, and "than" belongs with comparatives such as "larger" or "slower".
why.B: "Different from" is the standard idiom, and the two things compared sit on either side of it.
why.C: "Different to" is British usage rather than the American standard the test follows.
why.D: "Than that of" adds a comparison to a possessed thing, which leaves "the older ones" with nothing to belong to.

context: A rain garden is a shallow depression planted with deep-rooted species «, that takes runoff from a roof and lets it soak in.»

choices.text: that takes runoff from a roof and lets it soak in.
which takes runoff from a roof, and lets it soak in.
, that takes runoff from a roof, and lets it soak in.

why.A: A clause beginning with "that" is essential to the noun it modifies, and an essential clause never takes a comma before it.
why.B: No comma before "that", and none before "and", which joins two verbs sharing the same subject.
why.C: Switching to "which" would need a comma before it, and the comma before "and" wrongly splits a compound predicate.
why.D: This keeps the comma that does not belong before "that" and adds a second one that does not belong before "and".

context: The principle worked in the narrow sense that the water «left, what it produced downstream» was a different matter.

why.A: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone is a comma splice.
why.B: A period ends the first sentence and starts the second, which is the simplest correct repair.
why.C: The extra comma turns the second subject into an apparent interruption and leaves the splice in place.
why.D: Removing the punctuation makes "what it produced downstream" the object of "left", which says the water left something behind rather than departing.

context: Slow-water design has one economic feature municipal budgets are not built for«: it is cheap to build and expensive to maintain.»

choices.text: ; that it is cheap to build and expensive to maintain.
, : it is cheap to build and expensive to maintain.

Yes, because it explains in detail how a harpsichord responds to changes in the humidity of the room it is standing in.
No, because Huang says he would not do anything differently.
No, because the passage concerns a single builder rather than the trade as a whole.

why.A: That sentence names both halves of the question directly — universal agreement and near-universal exception — and the 1986 instrument is the case that shows it.
why.B: The humidity explains why the problem exists, not why the principle goes unfollowed.
why.C: He says the opposite: he would make the soundboard thicker and accept a smaller sound.
why.D: One builder is how the passage makes its point, and Huang states the principle in general terms.
